audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding sentence is verbatim on Gradin 1966 p.46 sec. 6, confirmed on the scanned of the sealang page scan; the record's 'held' list was empty, so the PDF was re-downloaded and (2) Deciding source: a 1966 SIL phonemics article, the only phonological description of Jeh proper in Glottolog's 21-item bibliography; Gradin 1976 (downloaded) restates the monosyllable + CV-presyllable structure, and Person 2022 (downloaded via the Internet Archive; the live UND repository is behind an automated-access block) documents the same reduced-presyllable + main-syllable shape for the closely related Li Xei lect. Nothing found contradicts 'fixed-dominant, final (main-syllable) stress, max two syllables'. (3) list of works to obtain is short and low-priority: the 1979 Jeh vocabulary and 1976 language lessons are the only unheld Jeh-specific items that could add

sources.citation: Gradin 1966, Consonantal tone in Jeh phonemics, MKS 2:41-53, p.46 sec.6 (PDF re-downloaded from sealang.net MKS archive, page scan read). Sesquisyllabic: max 2 syllables, stress always on final (main) syllable.
sources.quote: The word in Jeh can be defined as having one main syllable, which may be preceded by an unstressed, but occasionally morphologically significant, presyllable.

sources.citation: Person, Stephanie Lynn. 2022. Li Xei: A phonology of an understudied Bahnaric language in central Vietnam. MA thesis, University of North Dakota. xv+171 pp.
sources.quote: Li Xei (closely related to Jeh, not Jeh proper): 'The syllable structure of Li Xei is essentially monosyllabic... Li Xei words can also include an optional pre-syllable (CP v), which consists of a consonant and a reduced vowel... pronounced as a very short or light vowel, or not at all... they are still always shorter than the vowel of the main syllable.' Pre-syllables 'often greatly reduced' or 'left off completely'. The word 'stress' is never used; prominence asymmetry (reduced presyllable vs full main syllable) is consistent with main/final-syllable prominence.
sources.locator: sec. 3.1 Syllable Structure, pp.7-9; classification p.1

sources.citation: Gradin, Dwight. 1976. Word affixation in Jeh. Mon-Khmer Studies 5:25-42.
sources.quote: 'Basically words in Jeh are monosyllabic. Disyllabic words do occur, but are relatively infrequent. The first syllable of disyllabic words is considered to be a presyllable... The language employs only eight presyllables, all of a CV variety.' Also: 'presyllables are often dropped in some dialects.'

sources.citation: Gradin, Dwight. 1966. Consonantal tone in Jeh phonemics. Mon-Khmer Studies 2:41-53.
sources.quote: 'The word in Jeh can be defined as having one main syllable, which may be preceded by an unstressed, but occasionally morphologically significant, presyllable.' Sec. 6.1: presyllable is C V with the vowel neutralised to a (i after j/s).

sources.note: Silent on stress. The catalog record is rule '01' (an earlier compilation-2026-08-31), i.e. in the presyllable + main-syllable disyllable the second (main, final) syllable is stressed. Gradin 1976's presyllable/main-syllable framing is consistent with that but is not a stress statement, so it neither confirms nor refutes the record. download note:http://purl.org/sealang/gradin1976word.pdfredirects tohttp://sealang.net/gradin1976word.pdf,which refused connection on both attempts (port 80 connection refused; https no response) on 2026-09-17; the file read is the copy saved from archives.sealang…

sources.citation: Cohen, Patrick D. 1966. Presyllables and reduplication in Jeh. Mon-Khmer Studies 2:31-40 (sealang bundle 2:31-53).
sources.quote: Describes presyllable inventory (pa-, ta-, ka-, al-, ma-, ja-, si-, ?a-) before the main syllable; defers to Gradin sec. 6.1 for structure; no explicit stress statement (a full-text search for stress/accent all pages: no 'stress').

sources.citation: Nguyễn Đăng Châu. 2008. Cơ cấu ngữ âm tiếng Bh'noong (trong ngôn ngữ Giẻ-Triêng) [The phonetic structure of Bh'noong (within the Giẻ-Triêng language)]. Báo cáo tổng kết đề tài cấp Bộ, mã số B2007-ĐN03-23. Đà Nẵng: Bộ Giáo dục & Đào tạo, Đại học Đà Nẵng. (Report with c.1600-item Bh'noong-Vietnamese-English wordlist; English summary 'Bh'noong Dialect's phonological-phonetic structure (in Gie-Trieng language)'.)
sources.note: Full text (HTML) read: phonological word = presyllable + stressed main syllable; consonant system retains breathy-voiced stops /b d/ ('giọng thở') in older speakers; explicitly calls Bh'noong 'a language that has not (yet) formed tone', contrasting it with tonalized Mon-Khmer sisters; mentions prenasalization and glottalization as further phonetic features; a dedicated prosody section I.4 (pp.42-51) exists in the print report but is not online.

tone.quote: Là một ngôn ngữ chưa hình thành thanh điệu, hệ thống phụ âm tiếng Bh’noong chắc chắn mang trong mình nó những đặc trưng cổ xưa mà những ngôn ngữ anh em trong gia đình Môn – Khmer thanh điệu hóa từng có.
tone.locator: ch. I, sec. I.3.2.3.1 'Đặc trưng tổng quát' (last sentence, immediately before heading I.3.2.3.2 'Các tiêu chí khu biệt'); HTML reproduction, no page numbers
tone.translation: Being a language that has not (yet) developed tone, the consonant system of Bh'noong certainly carries within it the archaic features that its tonalized sister languages in the Mon-Khmer family once had.
tone.summary: No tone (Bh'noong variety); breathy-voiced stop series; stress on main syllable.

Bundoora, Vic.: Linguistics Program, La Trobe University. (ISSN 1036-0808; La Trobe OPAL record dates it 1994-07-01, '© The Author 1994'; Glottolog ref 15058 gives 1995.) DOI 10.26181/22201852.v1

sources.note: Repository abstract only: Mon-Khmer historical phonologists complain of poor vowel correspondences; in Bahnaric, low-level reconstructions (Proto-Jeh-Halang) were made first and then compared to build Proto-North-Bahnaric, which propagates low-level errors upward; the paper argues this happened and proposes a revision of Proto-Jeh-Halang and Proto-North-Bahnaric VOWELS. Tone/register is not mentioned in the abstract; whether Jeh's laryngealized ('deep') vowel series or Gradin's consonantal tone figures in the revision is unverified.

sources.note: Seen only through Nguyễn Đăng Châu 2008's Vietnamese quotation of it: at the common Jeh-Halang stage there was no length contrast before zero vs glottal-fricative /h/ finals; the lax, breathy vowel /e/ did not combine with voiceless-stop finals; the lax, breathy glide /ie/ occurred only before /k, ŋ, h/ - i.e. the reconstruction works with a lax/breathy vs clear vowel (register) distinction and laryngeal finals. What the article says about the Jeh 'consonantal tone' reflex itself was not seen by S or C.
